concept: lexical base distinguished from inflectional forms
statement: A lexical base is the reference form from which the inflectional paradigm is described; it is distinct from any individual inflectional form even though one or more inflected forms often coincide with the base.
condition: For a variable lexeme, identify its lexical base separately from its attested singular, plural or other inflectional forms; a defective lexeme can have a base for which no corresponding independent form exists, and several forms can coincide with the base.

exceptions.description: Defective lexemes may lack a surface form corresponding to the lexical base; several inflectional forms can also be identical to the lexical base.

contrast.text: The dregs settled at the bottom. [plural-only noun, with a lexical base dreg- not used as a plain singular form]
One sheep escaped through the fence. [singular coincides with the lexical base]
Several sheep escaped through the fence. [plural also coincides with the same lexical base]
A worker greeted the visitors. [the singular matches the lexical base of worker]

concept: inflection of simple and complex lexical bases
statement: In English, a lexeme's base can be internally simple or morphologically complex, and regular inflectional operations generally apply to either kind without changing their basic formation rules.
condition: When a noun's lexical base is simple (e.g., dog) or consists of morphological units (e.g., worker), apply the ordinary plural suffixation operation to the complete lexical base, rather than treating internal derivational complexity as a reason for a different plural rule.

Two workers waited outside the office. [complex base worker, regular plural]
The trainer hired three workers. [inflection attaches to the whole complex lexical base]
